title: Fear Versus Promise When Communicating Major Change
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the choice leaders face when announcing major organizational change: appeal to fear of what happens if the change fails, or appeal to the promise of what's possible if it succeeds. It argues that fear appeals, while they can create short-term urgency, ultimately backfire — they raise anxiety and defensiveness, cause people to downplay risks and demand more justification, and erode trust, sometimes hardening into an 'us versus them' dynamic. Promise-based messaging, by contrast, builds trust, invites collaboration in planning the change, and earns more durable commitment because people want to help build a better future rather than avoid a worse one.
points: Leaders face a choice when communicating change: emphasize the threat of not changing, or the promise of what change enables.
Fear appeals create short-term urgency but research shows they ultimately backfire.
Fear-based messaging breeds anxiety, defensiveness, skepticism, and an 'us versus them' dynamic.
Promise-based messaging builds trust and invites genuine collaboration in planning the change.
People commit more durably to a positive vision of the future than to avoiding a threatened loss.
quotes: Because leaders themselves often fear the cold reality of what it would mean not to make the change, they often appeal to fear instead of promise.
Unfortunately, research proves that choosing fear is the wrong call and has its own disastrous consequences.
Fear appeals about change lead to anxiety, stress, and highly defensive reactions.
The better call for leaders communicating change is to paint a picture of a more positive and different future.
They abhor being told that if they don’t change, their world is all but lost. Fear is self-defeating.
